projects.title: Purchasing Platform
projects.subtitle: From icon-only navigation and broken search URLs to a structured, AI-powered procurement experience.
projects.client: A B2B procurement SaaS serving mid-market and enterprise buyers across North America
projects.team: Cross-functional team of 6 (Product, Engineering, QA, Marketing)
challenge: The platform had a powerful AI search engine (HawkSearch) under the hood and no experience to match it. Navigation was a row of unlabeled icons. Search generated broken, dead-end URLs. The platform's most powerful feature — AI search across purchase histories, warranties, and supplier catalogs — was invisible to users and unknown to most of the team.
The mandate: make what exists work, introduce proven e-commerce patterns, then design the leap — an AI-native procurement experience.

work.title: Design System
work.problem: 40+ button variants, no shared visual language, and every new feature compounding the inconsistency.
work.solution: A token-first design system built in Figma — primitives through templates, every component documented with interaction states and responsive specs.

work.title: Mobile Experience
work.problem: No responsive foundation — broken layouts, inaccessible touch targets, and purchasing flows that punished mobile users.
work.solution: A mobile-first rebuild of the full journey — discovery, cart, checkout, support, and account — modeled on proven e-commerce patterns. Task completion rose across every flow.

work.title: Platform Navigation
work.problem: “Buying Desk” opened a quote form. “Vendors” led to info pages. Everything else was an unlabeled icon — and the storefront and admin ran on two different design systems.
work.solution: Labeled, hierarchy-first navigation with breadcrumbs, unified across storefront and admin. One coherent product instead of two disconnected ones.

work.title: Shopping Experience
work.problem: Refrigerators filed under “Anchors & Setup.” Broken search URLs. 83% mobile cart abandonment and an 85% exit rate right after purchase.
work.solution: A rebuilt taxonomy that matches how buyers search, clean faceted-search URLs, product pages that build buying confidence, and a streamlined checkout — with HawkSearch reworked into rapid, navigable results.

work.title: Platform Redesign
work.problem: The quick wins proved the platform could work — but they were still patches on an aging foundation.
work.solution: A ground-up reimagining: full design-system overhaul plus mid-fi and hi-fi concepts for a search-first, AI-native procurement experience. Demonstrated to stakeholders and strongly received; cut before shipping by a market downturn.

validation: Heuristic evaluation against Nielsen's 10 usability principles
Tree testing of the restructured navigation taxonomy
Moderated usability sessions on search and registration flows
WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility audit before handoff
iteration: Redesign concepts demonstrated to the full stakeholder group
HawkSearch AI capabilities documented and socialized internally
URL and breadcrumb patterns set as platform standards

metrics.label: Component variants consolidated into a single system

projects.summary: The platform's AI was genuinely competitive — what was missing was the UX scaffolding to make it usable. Each workstream added a layer: a design system, mobile foundations, real navigation, and a validated vision for an AI-native future.

projects.title: Greenridge Naturals
projects.subtitle: A ground-up rebrand and e-commerce overhaul — 420% sales growth and 230% traffic growth in twelve months.
projects.client: Greenridge Naturals — a DTC wellness brand scaling fast on an outdated identity
projects.team: Solo designer leading a cross-functional team (Dev, Operations, Marketing)
challenge: No design system, a 9-step checkout with 78% mobile abandonment, zero SEO metadata or conversion tracking, and shipping misconfiguration bleeding $4–8 of margin on every order.
As sole design and digital lead reporting directly to the CEO, I owned brand, UX, front-end, platform migration, SEO, and marketing in a 12-month ground-up rebuild.

work.title: Brand & Design System
work.problem: A legacy identity applied inconsistently across packaging, web, and social — undermining credibility at every touchpoint.
work.solution: A rebuilt brand on a clean typographic foundation, systematized in Figma: brand tokens, product cards, collection grids, banners, and subscription UI — all responsive, all documented.

work.title: Site Architecture
work.problem: Product discovery was a flat category list — no filtering, no search logic, no merchandising.
work.solution: Catalog reorganized around three consumer need states — Daily Wellness, Targeted Support, Bundles & Value — with faceted filtering and best-sellers surfaced at the top level.

work.title: Checkout & Conversion
work.problem: Nine checkout steps, no guest option — 78% mobile cart abandonment.
work.solution: Checkout compressed to 4 steps with guest-first default. In testing, every participant completed purchase in under 3 minutes versus 8+ on the legacy flow.

work.title: Platform & Growth Engine
work.problem: No structured SEO, no conversion tracking, and misconfigured shipping costing $4–8 per order.
work.solution: Headless Shopify migration with Klaviyo, GA4 + GTM, ShipBob (corrected zone logic), and Yotpo — every integration mapped to a specific conversion or retention objective.

validation: Moderated usability testing on the redesigned checkout (n=6)
Tree testing of new navigation — 94% found products within 2 clicks
Technical SEO audit; schema markup on 100% of product pages
Cross-device QA across 12 device/browser combinations
iteration: GA4 + GTM event tracking across the full funnel
Klaviyo automations: abandoned cart, post-purchase, win-back, welcome
Monthly SEO content calendar targeting high-intent keywords
Quarterly Hotjar heatmap and session-recording reviews
projects.summary: Brand, funnel, backend, and acquisition rebuilt simultaneously — compounding returns no isolated fix could produce.

projects.title: Building Hoists.com
projects.subtitle: From no digital presence to $1.2M in year one — now $12M a year. Built by learning an industry from scratch.
projects.client: Sievert Crane & Hoist — the DTC arm, built from zero
projects.team: Scaled from solo to a 5-person department (UX, Content, Development, Operations)
challenge: No catalog, no product data — just 3,500+ SKUs in an ERP and a sales team that knew the product cold. Industrial buyers are deeply technical, and every spec matters. The filter UI exposed every value as its own checkbox — buyers averaged 5,000–10,000 page visits to find the right product.
As founding digital lead reporting to the President, I was solo designer, developer, and strategist for 18 months, then scaled the department to five.

work.title: Domain Immersion
work.problem: I knew e-commerce, not hoists — and product knowledge lived only in PDF spec sheets, ERP line items, and people's heads.
work.solution: Ran between sales, mechanics, techs, and metal fabricators to learn the domain firsthand — then built the entire catalog around real buyer mental models instead of the spec sheet.

work.title: Catalog Architecture
work.problem: No taxonomy for 3,500+ SKUs spanning hoists, cranes, trolleys, and accessories.
work.solution: A five-tier hierarchy — Product Family → Type → Capacity Class → Configuration → Variant — with smart filter logic suppressing incompatible combinations in real time.

work.title: Smart Range Filters
work.problem: Every spec value was a standalone checkbox — lift heights from 1ft up, capacities to 20,000 lbs. Hundreds of options, no grouping, 5,000–10,000 visits per purchase.
work.solution: Hundreds of checkboxes collapsed into intelligent capacity and height ranges that match how buyers think — light, medium, heavy industrial. Average purchase journey: two visits.

work.title: AI Chat & ERP Integration
work.problem: Technical questions bottlenecked on the sales team. Freight quotes took 48 hours. Availability changed daily through pandemic supply chaos.
work.solution: An AI chat tool answering spec questions in real time, Epicor ERP sync for live inventory and lead times, and cart-level LTL freight via Freightquote.

validation: Domain immersion with sales, mechanics, techs, and fabricators
Tree testing of the 5-tier taxonomy — 91% task success
Cognitive walkthroughs with maintenance managers and procurement officers
ERP data QA across 3,500+ SKUs before launch
iteration: AI chat iterated continuously from real buyer questions
Monthly technical SEO content — organic traffic +600% in 18 months
Support-ticket analysis drove two major IA iterations
Quarterly buyer interviews as the catalog expanded
projects.summary: One decision changed everything: make the filters match how buyers think, not how the spec sheet is organized. $1.2M in year one, $2M in year two, $12M annually now — that's information architecture compounding.

projects.title: Cards in Bars
projects.subtitle: A party game for bars. Your phone is your hand, the TV is the table, and there is nothing to install.
projects.client: Personal product — first venue is Innjoy in Logan Square, with its own deck of local cards
projects.team: Solo — design, front end, back end, deployment
challenge: A Cards Against Humanity–style party game built for bars. The venue puts a QR and a permanent code on a TV; patrons scan it, type a name, and are dealt in from their own phone.

The core problem: split one game across two surfaces — a private phone and a public screen — so each shows what its audience needs and nothing it shouldn't. In a loud room, ten feet from the TV, with a drink in one hand.

work.title: Getting in without an app
work.problem: Nobody installs an app to play one round. Every second between seeing the TV and holding cards is a chance to give up.
work.solution: A permanent per-venue code and QR, printable on a table tent. Scanning drops you into the game; the only required step is a name. Accounts are optional and use a recovery code, not an email and password.

work.title: Two screens, one game
work.problem: The phone is private, the TV is public. Show the wrong thing on either and the round is ruined — a leaked hand, or a shared moment trapped on one screen.
work.solution: Each surface gets a different payload. Phones get their own hand and nothing else; the TV gets public state on a read-only channel.

work.title: Designing for ten feet
work.problem: The TV was designed at desk distance. Supporting copy sat at 21px on a 1080p panel, and the QR — the only thing that turns a stranger into a player — had a third of the screen while a demo took two thirds.
work.solution: A viewport-height type scale with a ~24px floor at 1080p, and a nested bento layout with the QR as the hero tile.

work.title: The review that found real bugs
work.problem: The work had gone reactive — spot something, fix that one thing. Functional tests only prove code does what it was told to.
work.solution: A screen-by-screen pass in player order, judged against measured values. It found a written card destroyed when a judge disconnected, a sheet advertising a swipe that did not exist, and an idle TV claiming someone was playing to an empty room.

validation: A headless harness drives real games over sockets — 23 assertions covering the deal, rotation, round expiry, discards and the 20-round cap
A screen-by-screen design review of all 12 player screens and the TV, judged against measured values rather than impressions
Killed the server mid-round in production to confirm the table and every phone recovered
iteration: Deployed on a persistent host with a mounted volume — games survive restarts and deploys
A Playwright rig drives a real game and photographs both surfaces, so every screenshot regenerates in one command
Next: the bar-facing admin screens, and a first full night at Innjoy
projects.summary: Reviewing an interface properly turned out to be quality control, not decoration — walking every screen in the order a player meets it found three real bugs that functional tests had missed. Building it alone meant every design decision had to survive contact with the system implementing it.

projects.title: AllG Fabrication
projects.subtitle: Moving a 30-year manufacturer from catalog-and-call ordering to true e-commerce — traffic up nearly 500%.
projects.client: AllG Fabrication (Argyle, TX) — founded in 1987 as Advanced Lightning Technology, manufacturing for wireless carriers, lightning protection and grounding systems, and custom fabrication
projects.team: AllG's internal tech team (development) and Bella Group (creative & marketing)
challenge: AllG sold through a traditional catalog shopping experience: browse a product list, then contact a sales rep to actually buy. The mandate was to redesign the website as a modern e-commerce experience — one that had to run on the company's custom ASP.NET framework and be built by their internal tech team.
I led brand design, wireframing of the new site, prototyping, and all UX/UI design, research, and testing.

work.title: Brand Design
work.problem: A manufacturer with three distinct competencies — wireless-carrier manufacturing, lightning protection systems, and custom fabrication — needed an identity that presented them as one modern company online.
work.solution: Led the brand design for the new site, working alongside Bella Group on the broader creative and marketing effort.

work.title: From Catalog to Storefront
work.problem: Products lived in a catalog structure that assumed a sales rep would close every sale.
work.solution: Wireframed the new site's architecture from scratch, restructuring the product lines into a browsable, purchasable e-commerce experience.

work.title: Prototype, Test, Hand Off
work.problem: The build would happen on a custom ASP.NET framework by AllG's internal team — the design had to be validated and unambiguous before a line of code was written.
work.solution: High-fidelity Adobe XD prototypes, backed by UX research and testing, carried the design through stakeholder sign-off and into development.

validation: UX research and usability testing across the redesign
High-fidelity Adobe XD prototype used for sign-off and developer handoff

metrics.label: Of purchases now completable online — no sales rep required
Surge in site traffic after launch
Revenue growth in the first year post-launch

projects.summary: The redesign turned a contact-a-rep catalog into a self-serve storefront: visitors can now complete 100% of their purchases online, traffic surged nearly 500%, and the business grew roughly 15% in revenue in the first year after launch.

projects.title: TEDxChicago 2026 — We The People
projects.subtitle: A fully custom event landing page, hand-coded and shipped inside Squarespace's constraints.
projects.client: TEDxChicago — the 2026 “We The People” event at the Harris Theater, Millennium Park (Oct 3, 2026)
challenge: TEDxChicago's site runs on Squarespace, but the 2026 event deserved a page the platform's templates couldn't produce — a bold, custom identity for the “We The People” theme with dot-matrix display type, the TEDx red quote-mark motif, and full creative control over layout and motion.
The constraint: it still had to live inside Squarespace — same domain, same nav and footer, editable by the team — without a separate host or framework.

work.title: The page
work.problem: Squarespace templates couldn't deliver the event's visual identity or the layout control the design called for.
work.solution: A hand-coded vanilla HTML/CSS/JS page — hero, speakers, tickets, FAQ — with all styles scoped under a single root element so nothing leaks into or out of the surrounding Squarespace chrome.

work.title: The deployment pipeline
work.problem: Squarespace only accepts pasted code blocks, and pasting a whole page on every change doesn't scale.
work.solution: A build script that strips the local dev chrome and emits a paste-ready embed, with CSS, JS, and assets served from the public GitHub repo via jsDelivr's CDN — so most changes ship with a git push and a cache purge, no Squarespace edits at all.

work.title: Working within CDN limits
work.problem: jsDelivr caps files at 20 MB, caches for 12 hours, and is case-sensitive — easy ways to break a live event page.
work.solution: Large source masters stay out of the repo with optimized web derivatives committed instead, cache-busting is versioned, and the purge step is part of the deploy routine.

validation: Every change verified on the live Squarespace embed, not just locally
CSS scoped with :where() to the page root — zero style collisions with Squarespace's own chrome
Structured data (JSON-LD event markup) for search
iteration: Speaker lineup section built and held ready to ship the moment the lineup is announced
Content updates ship via git push + CDN purge — no developer needed for copy changes in Squarespace blocks
projects.summary: The page is live at tedxchicago.com powering the 2026 event — a custom-designed, hand-coded experience running invisibly inside a template platform, with a deploy pipeline the team can live with.

projects.title: Floofer
projects.subtitle: Swipe. Match. Save a life. An adoption app that surfaces the dogs closest to running out of time.
projects.team: Solo — product, design system, and front end
challenge: Adoption sites rank dogs by recency and photogenics — which buries the dogs at highest euthanasia risk exactly when visibility matters most. Floofer inverts that: the deck surfaces at-risk dogs first, each carrying a visible days-remaining badge.
The second inversion: match on fit, not cuteness. Sixty seconds of onboarding — home, yard, kids, other pets, experience — lets the app rank dogs by how well they'd actually fit your home.

work.title: Urgency-first discovery
work.problem: Time-critical dogs get the same shelf position as every other listing.
work.solution: A swipe deck ordered by risk, with a prominent countdown badge on every at-risk profile — chosen specifically because the RescueGroups.org API exposes euthanasia-date fields most aggregators ignore.

work.title: A real design system first
work.problem: Solo side projects usually skip the system and pay for it at every screen.
work.solution: A full Figma library built before the screens: variables with dark/light modes mapped to CSS custom properties, and components for cards, chips, badges, pickers, navigation, and empty states — the app is assembled from it, not drawn ad hoc.

work.title: Kind interaction rules
work.problem: One mis-tap on a 'pass' is a dog someone never sees again.
work.solution: No destructive one-tap actions, full-screen pickers instead of fiddly dropdowns, and compact cards tuned through repeated hands-on preview passes.

validation: Playwright smoke suite covering the core flows
Iterative element-by-element UX passes in live preview
Server-side proxies built for RescueGroups.org and Petfinder, with demo data powering development
iteration: Next: live shelter data keys, then a public beta deploy
Design system documented with a full rebuild procedure in the repo
projects.summary: An app with a thesis: visibility should follow urgency, and matches should follow fit. Built system-first — the Figma library and its dark/light token modes came before the first screen, and every component in the app traces back to it.
